rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 and Tables 4-7 report the authors' own greenhouse experiment (Tongzhou station, 2016) with micro-nano bubble water oxygation via subsurface drip on tomato and cucumber, nine treatments, four replicates.
rows.notes: The passage claims ADI conserves soil moisture and saves water and fertilizer. The study held irrigation quota and fertilizer identical across all treatments (Section 2.2, Table 3) and did not measure soil moisture or any water or fertilizer saving; it assumed soil water content and evaporation were approximately equal across treatments (Section 3.2). What it shows is higher yield and therefore higher IWUE at the same water input (Table 5), which is an efficiency result, not a water-saving or soil-moisture-conservation result. Reviewer doubt: a lenient reader might treat the IWUE gain as water-conservation evidence; rated no because the claimed effect (water/fertilizer saving, soil moisture) was not tested.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 and Tables 4-7 report the authors' own greenhouse experiment with micro-nano bubble water oxygation through subsurface drip irrigation on tomato and cucumber in spring and autumn 2016.
rows.notes: The passage claims better water conservation. The study applied identical irrigation amounts in all treatments (Table 3) and did not measure water saved or soil water; it reports irrigation water use efficiency (Table 5), which rose only because yield rose at fixed water input (Section 3.2 states the IWUE trend was the same as yield for this reason). No water-conservation outcome was tested. Doubt noted: IWUE is sometimes used as a proxy for water conservation, but the effect named in the passage was not measured.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3, own greenhouse field experiment with nine MNBWO treatments, four replicates, two crops, two seasons. Q2: Table 5 and Section 3.2 report tomato and cucumber yields significantly higher under micro-nano bubble oxygation through SDI than the groundwater-only control, e.g. tomato yield in M1/4 at F1/5 was 16.9% higher than M0/1 and cucumber M1/0 was 22.1% higher at F1/5; Section 4.1 summarises tomato yield increases of 7.8-26.9% and cucumber 2.3-16.3%. Q4: Section 2.3.3 and Fig. 3 report measured soil oxygen content under the three mixing ratios, showing MNBWO raised root-zone soil oxygen and kept it stable within 24 h after oxygation, the mechanism invoked for yield gain in Section 4.1; Table 4 also reports measured root and shoot dry matter. Q9: Table 5 gives yield means with <U+00B1> dispersion values for every treatment and season.
rows.notes: Q3 no: yield measured by a single harvest method. Q5 no: one greenhouse site, one loam soil, two crops, two seasons. Q6 no: 6 m x 3 m plots in one greenhouse. Q7 no: authors recommend optimal mixing ratios and a 5-day frequency and speculate why 7-day frequency performs worse (Section 4.4), but these are optimisation gradients, not stated requirements for the yield effect to occur. Q8 no: the only limitation-type remarks concern fruit quality mechanism and the mixing-ratio gradient (Section 4.3) and untested autumn cucumber vitamin C, not the yield result. The technology is micro-nano bubble oxygation through SDI, a form of aerated drip irrigation as the review defines it.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3, own greenhouse experiment with MNBWO via subsurface drip, nine treatments, four replicates. Q2: Table 5 and Section 3.2 report both yield and irrigation water use efficiency of tomato and cucumber significantly higher under micro-nano bubble oxygation than the non-oxygated control (e.g. tomato IWUE 27.4 vs 24.6 kg/m3 at F1/5; cucumber IWUE 30.0 vs 23.7 kg/m3 at F1/5 in spring); abstract reports IWUE gains of 16.9% (tomato) and 22.1% (cucumber) in optimal treatments. Q4: Section 2.3.3 and Fig. 3 report measured root-zone soil oxygen content, higher and stable for 24 h under MNBWO, the intermediate variable the authors use to explain yield and IWUE gains (Section 4.1); Section 3.2 also explains the IWUE gain arises from yield at equal water input. Q9: Table 5 reports yield and IWUE with <U+00B1> dispersion for each treatment and season.
rows.notes: IWUE here is yield divided by a fixed irrigation quota, so the WUE gain is entirely a yield effect; the passage's WUE wording matches what the study reports. Q3 no: single method. Q5 no: one site, one soil, two crops. Q6 no: plot scale in one greenhouse. Q7 no: optimal ratio and frequency are recommended, not stated as conditions required for the effect. Q8 no: no limitation stated for the yield/IWUE result.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Supplementary figures on bubble size and dissolved oxygen are referenced but not included. The study is a single-site greenhouse experiment on loam soil with tomato and cucumber over spring and autumn 2016; irrigation and fertiliser inputs were identical across treatments, so results bear on yield, IWUE and fruit quality rather than on water or fertiliser saving per se.
